title: An Ensemble Framework for Unbiased Language Model Watermarking
one_liner: Stack multiple independent watermarks on top of each other so the detection signal grows while the model's output stays unchanged.
lead: A watermark is a hidden fingerprint embedded in model output to prove who created it. Normal watermarks leave traces that change how the model talks, making generated text worse or easier to spot as fake. This paper stacks multiple watermarks together—each one tiny and harmless, but combined they make the fingerprint loud enough to detect while keeping the text exactly as good as unwatermarked output.

paras: When a language model generates text, it picks the next word by rolling weighted dice—some words are more likely, others less. To hide a watermark, you secretly re-weight those dice so certain words become slightly more likely. A detector later reads the text and asks: were these words picked with tampered dice? If they were, the watermark is real.

The hard part: you want the re-weighting to be unbiased—meaning the model's overall output should sound exactly the same whether watermarked or not. Why? Because if watermarked text sounds different, someone can strip the watermark by rewriting the text, and a human can spot watermarked text instantly, which defeats the point. But unbiased watermarks are weak. Each re-weighting is so tiny that it vanishes in the noise. A detector needs to read thousands of tokens to be confident the dice were tampered with—useless for short messages or when text gets paraphrased.

What a naive approach tries: make the watermark signal louder by re-weighting more aggressively. This fails because the louder the re-weighting, the more the model's output drifts from normal, and the quality drops.

callout.html: Stack independent watermarks so their signals pile up, boosting detection while keeping output unbiased.

steps.text: Apply watermark rule with key one: re-weight token probabilities, sample next word.
Feed the token probabilities from layer one into watermark rule with key two, apply same re-weighting.
Keep stacking: layer three, four, five, each with its own secret key, each a tiny adjustment.
Sample from the final stacked token probabilities as if it were any normal model output.
Compute detection score with each secret key separately, then add the scores together.

paras: The paper changes how many watermark layers get applied. Instead of one watermark, it stacks n independent watermarks in sequence, each with its own secret key. Each layer re-weights the model's token probabilities, then the next layer re-weights what came out of the first.
object.object: the number of stacked watermark layers

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: detection signal-to-noise ratio
hidden.name: Signal-to-noise ratio (how loud the watermark is relative to randomness)
paras: Every watermark produces a detection score—a number that should be high if the text is watermarked and low if it is not. But because text is noisy (some random words slip through), the score jiggles up and down. The signal-to-noise ratio is the strength of the pattern you are looking for divided by the amount of jiggling. A high ratio means the detector can confidently spot the watermark from short text. A low ratio means you need thousands of tokens.

The paper's key insight: when you stack n independent watermarks, their detection scores add up. The mean (average score) grows as n, but the noise (randomness) only grows as sqrt(n). So the signal-to-noise ratio grows as sqrt(n)—roughly the square root of the number of layers. This is the hidden quantity that makes ENS work.

heat.caption: Darker means higher watermark signal detected at this position; lighter means ambiguous or absent.

reads.html: The signal-to-noise ratio is like trying to hear a whisper in a crowd. One watermark is one whisper. Five watermarks are five people whispering the same thing in sync—the crowd noise does not grow five times, it only grows as the square root of five, so the whispers become much clearer.

When n independent watermarks are applied, the detection score aggregated across all keys has mean n times the per-key mean, variance n times the per-key variance. The math works out to: signal-to-noise ratio grows as the square root of n times the single-key ratio.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the layering trick
paras: Each unbiased watermark is a rule that re-weights the model's token probabilities slightly. Because it is unbiased, the re-weighting is so small that if you average over all possible random numbers in the watermark generator, the output distribution stays unchanged. The trick is: one watermark alone is so tiny that noise drowns it out. But stacking n watermarks does not make the output drift—each layer still applies an unbiased, tiny adjustment to what the previous layer gave it.

The magic happens in the detection. When you read the watermarked text, you run a detection test n times, once with each secret key. Each test finds a score: a number saying how watermark-like the text is. The scores from independent keys can be added together because they are measuring different pieces of evidence. When you add n scores, the true signal (from the real watermark) stacks and grows as n. But the false signal (randomness) only grows as the square root of n, because noise is independent. So the ratio improves by a factor of sqrt(n)—meaning detection becomes strong enough to work on very short text or text with minor edits, because the signal is now loud enough to cut through the noise even with fewer tokens to read.

stages.s: Watermark layer 1 with key one: tiny re-weighting
Watermark layer 2 with key two: another tiny re-weighting
Watermark layer 3 through n: repeat with new keys
Final distribution (still unbiased, watermark signal amplified)

math.words: total detection score = sum of all per-key scores; each per-key score measures how likely those tokens are under the watermarked distribution
math.equation: S_ENS(x1:T) = sum_i S(x1:T, sk_i); SNR_ENS = sqrt(n) times SNR_single

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose one watermark alone produces a detection score that is 10 units above random noise with noise level 2 units. Signal-to-noise ratio = 10 / 2 = 5.
Now stack 4 independent watermarks. Each produces a score 10 units above noise level 2.
Total signal = 4 times 10 = 40 units. Total noise = sqrt(4) times 2 = 4 units.
New signal-to-noise ratio = 40 / 4 = 10. This is sqrt(4) = 2 times better than one watermark alone.
Stacking 9 watermarks: signal = 90, noise = 6, ratio = 15, which is sqrt(9) = 3 times better. The square root law holds.

math.note: Each stacked layer contributes its detection score independently, and scores add up. Noise is random noise, so it only grows as the square root of the number of layers.

bars.h2: Detection performance: one vs. many layers

charts.title: One watermark layer
charts.note: One watermark is weak on short text; detection confidence (percent correct) jumps at medium length.

charts.title: Five stacked watermark layers
charts.note: Stacking layers shifts confidence high even at short text lengths, because the signal is now much stronger.

items.b: Too many layers runs out of space.
items.html: Each watermark nudges certain tokens up by a small amount. If you stack too many layers, those tokens run out of probability space (probabilities cannot exceed 1). At some point, adding more layers actually hurts because the re-weighting becomes impossible. The paper finds an optimal number of layers around 4-5 for typical settings.

items.b: Keys must be independent per generation step.
items.html: For the signal-to-noise math to work, each layer's random choices must be independent of the others. If the same random seed is used twice, the layers become correlated because they measure the same evidence twice, and you get no new information added—so the signal-to-noise ratio does not improve as sqrt(n) and you waste computational effort. The implementation must keep keys separate and uncorrelated.

If someone rewrites the text heavily, some watermarked tokens may be replaced with different words. More layers help because the watermark is spread across many tokens and only some are replaced, but if the text is rewritten so drastically that most watermarked tokens are gone, the detection score drops below the threshold even with a strong watermark, because you have fewer watermarked tokens to add up in the detection test.

items.b: Done right: carefully choose the number of layers.
items.html: Find the sweet spot where detection is strong but the probability space is not exhausted. Use independent keys for each layer. Test on short text to confirm the gain.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Generate text from a language model using ENS with different numbers of layers: one layer, two layers, four layers. For each, compute detection scores on sequences of different lengths (64 tokens, 256 tokens, 512 tokens). Plot how many tokens are needed to confidently detect the watermark as the number of layers increases. The demo should show that detection confidence grows from needing 500+ tokens with one layer to needing only 64 tokens with four layers.
demo.closing: The key finding: stacking watermark layers makes detection exponentially stronger—by a factor of sqrt(n)—because independent signals add up while noise only grows by its square root, and this gain costs nothing in text quality, which is the whole point.
